content: HIV testing can be integrated with diagnostic services for other diseases, such as sexually transmitted infections (STIs) and viral hepatitis. Diagnostic assays that lack good thermostability (unlike rapid diagnostic tests [RDTs], which can be stored between 4°C and 40°C) or require invasive specimen collection methods (e.g., venepuncture instead of capillary or fingerstick whole blood) are unsuitable for use in lower-tier healthcare settings (levels 0 and 1). For further details on assay formats for HIV diagnosis, refer to the WHO Consolidated Guidelines on HIV Testing Services (2019). Without this strategy, programs cannot reliably achieve such accuracy. The three-test strategy involves using three consecutive reactive HIV tests to confirm a positive diagnosis. This approach applies to individuals aged 18 months and older and excludes the use of Western blot and line immunoassays, which WHO advises against. The WHO's essential in vitro diagnostics list (EDL) outlines assays for common diseases and infections that can be used in both community settings without clinical laboratories and healthcare facilities with laboratory capabilities. Assay formats include immunoassays (IA), laboratory-based nucleic acid testing (Lab-NAT), point-of-care nucleic acid testing (POC-NAT), and rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs), including HIV self-testing (HIVST). Testing strategies for HIV diagnosis involve a sequence of tests designed to achieve specific objectives, such as infection screening or diagnosis. Additional data, such as PPV and negative predictive value (NPV), are needed to assess the predictive accuracy of assays within a testing algorithm. PPV represents the proportion of individuals with positive results who are correctly diagnosed with HIV, while NPV reflects the proportion of individuals with negative results who are correctly identified as HIV-negative. Unlike sensitivity and specificity, PPV and NPV are influenced by the prevalence of the disease in the population being tested. To achieve a PPV of at least 99%, WHO recommends selecting tests with a minimum sensitivity of 99% and specificity of 98%. In the three-test strategy, the first test (Assay 1) should have the highest sensitivity to identify all HIV-positive individuals, even if it includes some false positives. The second and third tests (Assays 2 and 3) must have very high specificity to rule out false positives from the first test. These three assays should be distinct products with minimal overlap in false reactivity. If discrepancies arise (e.g., Assay 1 is reactive, but Assay 2 is non-reactive), Assay 1 should be repeated to confirm reactivity. Individuals with repeated reactive results on Assay 1 but inconclusive results on subsequent tests should be classified as having an HIV-inconclusive status and retested after 14 days. Countries transitioning to the three-test strategy must align changes in procurement, algorithm verification, training, and policy updates. For example, Malawi adopted the three-test strategy in 2019 to maintain a PPV of at least 99%. An analysis revealed that this approach prevented the misdiagnosis of at least 371 individuals in 2023, avoiding unnecessary lifelong treatment and reducing healthcare costs. For children aged 18 months or younger, serological assays like HIV RDTs are insufficient for diagnosis due to the potential detection of maternal antibodies transferred during pregnancy. Virological testing, typically using nucleic acid testing (NAT), is recommended for this age group. HIV-exposed infants should undergo NAT at birth, 4–6 weeks, 9 months, and 18 months (or 3 months after breastfeeding cessation). Testing should also be conducted if the child presents with illness. A final diagnosis is only confirmed after the risk of transmission has ended. Retesting is critical in several scenarios, including resolving inconclusive results, verifying HIV-positive status before initiating antiretroviral therapy (ART), and re-engaging individuals in care. Retesting should ideally occur at a different site using a different lot of test kits. For individuals on ART, retesting is not recommended due to the potential for false-negative results caused by suppressed viral replication. However, some individuals on ART may still seek testing. In such cases, they should be informed about the limitations and risks of incorrect results. Serological assays are generally unaffected by ART, but false negatives are more likely in individuals who initiated ART during acute HIV infection or early infancy. Virological assays, such as NAT, may also yield undetectable results in individuals with suppressed viral loads, which does not rule out HIV infection. Only those with confirmed HIV-negative results should initiate PrEP or PEP. Retesting is recommended every 2–3 months or as needed when restarting PrEP. Reactive test results during PrEP or PEP use require further testing to confirm HIV status.
